{{Short description|Unsolved problem in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Hall's conjecture''' is an [[open problem|open question]] on the differences between [[square number|perfect squares]] and [[perfect cube]]s. It asserts that a perfect square ''<math>y^2</math>'' and a perfect cube ''<math>x^3</math>'' that are not equal must lie a substantial distance apart. This question arose from consideration of the [[Mordell equation]] in the theory of [[integer point]]s on [[elliptic curve]]s.

The original version of Hall's conjecture, formulated by [[Marshall Hall, Jr.]] in 1970, says that there is a positive constant ''<math>C</math>'' such that for any [[integer]]s ''<math>x</math>'' and ''<math>y</math>'' for which ''<math>y^2 \neq x^3</math>'',

:<math>|y^2 - x^3| > C|x|^{1/2}</math>.

Hall suggested that perhaps ''<math>C</math>'' could be taken as <math>1/5</math>, which was consistent with all the data known at the time the [[conjecture]] was proposed.

In 1982, [[Danilov (no wiki page)|Danilov]] proved that <math>|y^2-x^3|</math> is less than <math>433\sqrt{2}\times|x|^{1/2}</math> infinitely often,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Danilov |first=L. V. |date=September 1982 |title=Diophantine equation x3?y2=k and Hall's conjecture |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01140190 |journal=Mathematical Notes of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR |language=en |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=617–618 |doi=10.1007/BF01140190 |issn=0001-4346|url-access=subscription }}</ref> thus providing an upper bound on ''<math>C</math>'' and proving that the exponent <math>1/2</math> (that is, the use of <math>|x|^{1/2}</math>) is optimal and cannot be replaced by any higher power: for no <math>\delta > 0</math> is there a constant ''<math>C</math>'' such that <math>|y^2 - x^3| > C|x|^{1/2+\delta}</math> whenever <math>y^2 \neq x^3</math>.

In 1965, Davenport proved an analogue of the above conjecture in the case of [[polynomial]]s: if <math>f(t)</math> and ''<math>g(t)</math>'' are nonzero polynomials over the [[complex number]]s '''<math>\mathbb{C}</math>''' such that ''<math>g(t)^3\neq f(t)^2</math>'' in ''<math>\mathbb{C}[t]</math>'', then

:<math>\deg(g(t)^2 - f(t)^3) \geq \frac{1}{2}\deg f(t) + 1.</math>

The ''weak'' form of Hall's conjecture, stated by Stark and Trotter around 1980, replaces the [[square root]] on the right side of the [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] by any exponent ''less'' than <math>1/2</math>: for any ''<math>\varepsilon > 0</math>'', there is some constant ''<math>c(\varepsilon)</math>'' depending on ''<math>\varepsilon</math>'' such that for any integers ''<math>x</math>'' and ''<math>y</math>'' for which ''<math>y^2 \neq x^3</math>'',

:<math>|y^2 - x^3| > c(\varepsilon) |x|^{1/2 - \varepsilon}</math>.

The original, ''strong'', form of the conjecture with exponent <math>1/2</math> has never been disproved, although it is no longer believed to be true and the term ''Hall's conjecture'' now generally means the version with the ''<math>\varepsilon</math>'' in it.  For example, in 1998, [[Noam Elkies]] found the example

<math>447884928428402042307918^2 - 5853886516781223^3 = -1641843</math>,

for which compatibility with Hall's conjecture would require ''<math>C</math>'' to be less than ''<math>0.0214\approx1/50</math>'', so roughly 10 times smaller than the original choice of <math>1/5</math> that Hall suggested.

The weak form of Hall's conjecture would follow from the [[ABC conjecture]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Schmidt | first=Wolfgang M. | authorlink=Wolfgang M. Schmidt | title=Diophantine approximations and Diophantine equations | series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics | volume=1467 | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=1996 | edition=2nd | isbn=3-540-54058-X | zbl=0754.11020 | pages=205–206 }}</ref>  A generalization to other perfect powers is [[Pillai's conjecture]], though it is also known that Pillai's conjecture would be true if Hall's conjecture held for any specific ''<math>0<\varepsilon<1/2</math>''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nair |first=M |date=1 December 1977 |title=A NOTE ON THE EQUATION x^3−y^2=k |url=https://academic.oup.com/qjmath/article/29/4/483/1558203 |journal=The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=483–487|doi=10.1093/qmath/29.4.483 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
